Avenger of Blood
uh-VEN-jer uv BLUD
noun phrase (biblical institution)
From Hebrew go'el haddam ("redeemer of blood"); go'el is the kinsman-redeemer, the near relative whose duty it was to act on behalf of the family — here, to require the life of one who had shed a kinsman's blood.

See also: Avenger of Blood

Biblical Definition

The avenger of blood (Hebrew go'el haddam, "redeemer of blood") was the nearest male relative of a slain person, whose recognized duty under the Mosaic Law was to require the life of the killer — to see that the shedding of his kinsman's blood did not go unanswered. The institution rests on the deep biblical principle that human life is sacred because man is made in the image of God, so that the shedding of innocent blood demands a reckoning: "Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man" (Gen 9:6). The avenger of blood was the appointed human instrument of that reckoning. The same Hebrew word, go'el, is the kinsman-redeemer who buys back the family's land or person (as Boaz redeems Ruth) — the near relative who acts for the family's good; in the case of bloodshed, that family duty took the form of requiring justice for the slain. The Law carefully regulated the avenger: the cities of refuge protected the UNINTENTIONAL manslayer from him until a fair trial determined whether the killing was murder or manslaughter (Num 35; Deut 19; Josh 20). Thus the avenger's claim was real and just — blood was not cheap — but it was channeled through due process rather than left to private rage. The avenger of blood and the city of refuge together upheld both the sanctity of life (the claim of blood) and the justice of intent (the trial). Theologically, the avenger represents the law's just demand against the one who has incurred blood-guilt, the demand from which the sinner flees to Christ the refuge.

Webster 1828 Definition

The nearest kinsman (Hebrew go'el haddam) whose duty under the Law was to require the life of one who shed his relative's blood; grounded in the sanctity of life (Gen 9:6); regulated by the cities of refuge and a fair trial distinguishing murder from manslaughter.

AVENGER OF BLOOD, noun phrase. Hebrew go'el haddam ("redeemer of blood"); the nearest male kinsman of a slain person.

His recognized duty under the Mosaic Law: to require the life of the killer, so the shedding of kinsman's blood did not go unanswered.

Grounded in the sanctity of life: man bears God's image, so innocent blood demands a reckoning (Gen 9:6).

Regulated by the cities of refuge: the unintentional manslayer was protected until a fair trial distinguished murder from manslaughter.

Same word go'el as the kinsman-redeemer (e.g., Boaz); the family duty here took the form of requiring justice.

Key Scripture

Genesis 9:6 — "Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man."

Numbers 35:19 — "The revenger of blood himself shall slay the murderer: when he meeteth him, he shall slay him."

Numbers 35:24-25 — "Then the congregation shall judge between the slayer and the revenger of blood according to these judgments: And the congregation shall deliver the slayer out of the hand of the revenger of blood."

Deuteronomy 19:11-12 — "But if any man hate his neighbour, and lie in wait for him... then the elders of his city shall send and fetch him thence, and deliver him into the hand of the avenger of blood, that he may die."

Modern Corruption

The avenger of blood is corrupted when read as sanctioned private vengeance or blood-feud, when the sanctity-of-life principle behind it is dismissed, or when the careful legal regulation (cities of refuge, trial) is ignored so the institution appears more savage than it was.

expand to see more

Private-vengeance misreading. The avenger of blood is sometimes read as the law's endorsement of personal revenge — a license for the family to kill in rage. The Mosaic regulation tells against this: the cities of refuge interposed asylum and a trial; the congregation judged between the slayer and the avenger (Num 35:24-25); the unintentional manslayer was delivered from the avenger's hand; and only the convicted murderer was given over. The avenger was not a free agent of private vengeance but the appointed instrument of a regulated justice, restrained by due process. The institution channeled the family's legitimate claim through law, precisely to prevent the escalating blood-feuds that plagued cultures without such regulation.

Sanctity-of-life dismissal. Modern sensibilities, uneasy with capital punishment, may dismiss the whole institution as primitive bloodthirst. Its foundation is the opposite of bloodthirst: it is the conviction that human life is so sacred — because man bears God's image (Gen 9:6) — that the shedding of innocent blood cannot be shrugged off but demands a reckoning. The avenger of blood exists because blood is precious, not cheap. A society that no longer requires any reckoning for the shedding of innocent blood has not advanced beyond the avenger of blood; it has fallen below the value the institution placed on human life.
